Where every conic section lives

Hypercube Composition Theory. Circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola and the degenerate conics, placed on the plane dial, the k dial, the roundness dials and the shape dial. Blue is the no-wall (ellipse) type, magenta the one-wall (parabola) type, orange the two-wall (hyperbola) type.

DRAFT · Where every conic section lives in our framework

DRAFT, Nov 26 2026. Part of Hypercube Composition Theory (repo: fused-hyperoperation-algebra). Asked for by Brennan: look at all of the conic sections, not just one, since "the conics may already be hiding in the catalog as the dial itself." Builds on why-i/cayley-klein/ (κ = d − k²/4), polar-recast/ (section 3, the conics as the plane dial's shape), simplex/ (section 7, the shape dial), hypersphere/ (section 5) and gravity-from-theory/ (section N.3, Kepler). Checks: checks.py → checks_output.txt, 22 of 22 pass (sympy for the exact identities, numpy for the rest). Pictures: figures.py → figures/. No Lean in this pass (no Lean on this machine).

The answer in two sentences

Yes, the conics are the plane dial itself. Each setting (k, d) of the plane law is one conic, x² + kxy + dy² = y: ellipses fill the inside of the parabola d = k²/4, parabolas sit on it, hyperbolas fill the outside, and the old "chord rule" on that conic is exactly our law, with the walls where the conic runs off to infinity. The degenerate conics (point, double line, crossing lines) are where a number's size is 0, and the Cayley–Klein picture matches literally for one line's measure but not as "one conic per geometry", because ellipse, parabola and hyperbola are a single conic seen from different places.

Figure 0. Where every conic lives, by dial.

Figure 1. The (k, d) plane. Each dot's little box shows its conic. The magenta curve d = k²/4 is where the parabolas are, and it is itself a parabola. The dashed curves, lines of the same geometry κ = d − k²/4, are parabolas too.

A note on signs before the details. In the repo the plane number obeys ε² = kε − d, so with k = 0 it squares to −d. That is why d > 0 is the round (elliptic) side and d < 0 the hyperbolic side, the reverse of a convention that writes i² = d. The picture on the call ("positive, zero, negative look like hyperbolic, parabolic, elliptic") is right in the i² = d convention and flips in ours. Nothing else changes.

1. Every dial setting is one conic, and the chord rule on it is our law

Figure 2. Pick two points P and Q on the conic, draw the chord through them, then draw the line through O parallel to it. Where that line meets the conic again is P∘Q. Measured by the slope a of the line from O, this is exactly (a + b + kab)/(1 − dab).

Take the conic x² + kxy + dy² = y. It passes through the origin O, which plays the identity. The line y = a·x meets it once more, at P(a) = (a, a²)/(1 + ka + da²), so the slope a labels every point (A1).

  • The chord rule is our law, exactly (A2, sympy): the chord from P(a) to P(b) has slope (a + b + kab)/(1 − dab). So the line through O parallel to it lands on P(a ∘ b).
  • The conic is never degenerate (A3): its 3×3 matrix has determinant −1/4 for every (k, d).
  • Its type is the dial's region (A4): ellipse when k² − 4d < 0, parabola when k² − 4d = 0, hyperbola when k² − 4d > 0. The plane dial's discriminant k² − 4d is literally the conic discriminant B² − 4AC.
  • The walls are the conic's points at infinity (A5): the roots of 1 + ka + da² are the directions in which the conic runs off. Two walls = a hyperbola's two ends. One double wall = the single end of a parabola. No wall = an ellipse, which never leaves.
  • The dial's centre (0, 0) is the parabola y = x², and its chord rule is plain addition (A6).
  • The k line (d = 0) touches the parabola only at its tip. So every ∘ₖ law with real k ≠ 0 is a hyperbola, and its famous wall −1/k is one of the two asymptotes (the other is a = ∞). Relativity (0, −1/c²) and probability (k = −1, wall at certainty a = 1) are hyperbolas; the circle needs d or an imaginary k.

Known: the group law on a conic by chords (classical; a modern account is Lemmermeyer, "Conics, a poor man's elliptic curves", 2003), and the plane law with its discriminant (Coleman and McGuinness 1991). Ours: the one conic per dial setting, x² + kxy + dy² = y, whose chord rule is our law with the walls at infinity. It is the kind of fact that may be folklore, so treat it as a clean statement, not a discovery. Verdict: a real bridge. It answers the question directly: the dial plane is a map of the conics.

2. The "unit circle" of each plane number, and where the degenerate conics come from

Figure 3. Every plane number has a size N = x² + kxy + dy² that multiplies. After completing the square it reads X² + κY². Its levels 1, 0 and −1 give every conic centred at the origin, the degenerate ones included.

  • Size multiplies, and multiplying composes directions by our law (B1, B2). So the plane law is the law of the "unit circle" N = 1, read by direction a = y/x.
  • Completing the square is the Cayley map (B3). X = x + ky/2 turns N into X² + κY² with κ = d − k²/4, and the slope change it causes, a = T/(1 − (k/2)T), is exactly the Cayley map the Cayley–Klein page used. A two-line algebra fact, but it explains that page's formula: κ is what is left after completing the square.
  • Size 1: ellipse (circle after rescaling) when κ > 0; two parallel lines X = ±1 when κ = 0; hyperbola when κ < 0. So the flat setting's "unit circle" is not a parabola. It is a pair of parallel lines, and multiplying by 1 + tε slides along one of them (a Galilean shear) (B6). The parabola lives in section 1's conic instead, which is never centred.
  • Size 0 (the numbers you can't divide by): a single point when κ > 0, a double line when κ = 0 (the dual numbers' zero divisors), two crossing lines when κ < 0 (B4). Those crossing lines are the walls: the asymptotes of the unit hyperbola, the light cone of relativity (B5).
  • Size −1: nothing real for κ ≥ 0 (an "imaginary ellipse"); the other hyperbola for κ < 0.

Known: Yaglom's three kinds of plane numbers and their zero divisors (Yaglom, Complex Numbers in Geometry, 1968). Ours: the full 3 × 3 placement with the walls as the size-0 level. Verdict: unifies; every degenerate conic has a fixed home.

3. Cayley–Klein: literal for one line, not for the whole geometry

Figure 4. The law's ruler (its logarithm, the "hidden coordinate") is Cayley's projective distance with the two walls as the absolute points. It runs to infinity exactly at the walls.

Literal match. Cayley (1859) and Klein (1871) measure distance along a line by where the line meets a fixed conic, the absolute: two real points give hyperbolic measure (log of a cross-ratio), one double point gives parabolic measure, two imaginary points give elliptic measure (an angle). Our law's ruler ∫ da/(1 + ka + da²) is exactly this with the walls as the absolute points (C1): (1/√disc)·log of the cross-ratio of (a, 0) with the walls; log(1 + ka)/k for ∘ₖ; arctan with no real walls; a/(1 + ka/2) with a double wall. So the dial is literally Cayley's choice of measure on a line. This sharpens the Cayley–Klein page's "the hidden coordinate is the arc length".

Figure 5. Hilbert's distance inside a circle is the hyperbolic plane (Klein's model). Inside a parabola it is the same plane, with the same circles. A hyperbola gives it only with both branches together.

Not literal: "one conic per geometry".

  • The background on the call is right that an ellipse as the absolute, with Hilbert's distance, gives the hyperbolic disc (C2: matches the Klein-model formula on 30 random pairs).
  • But a parabola gives the same hyperbolic plane (C3: the distances agree to 10⁻⁶ after a projective map). In projective geometry ellipse, parabola and hyperbola are one conic. They differ only in how they meet the line at infinity: 0, 1 or 2 points, which is our wall count.
  • A hyperbola gives the hyperbolic plane only if you take the insides of both branches; one branch alone is half a disc and a different geometry (C4).
  • What does change the plane geometry in Cayley–Klein is the absolute itself: a real conic (hyperbolic plane, and de Sitter outside it), an imaginary conic (elliptic), or a degenerate one for the flat geometries (Euclidean: the line at infinity with two imaginary points on it; Minkowski: with two real points; Galilean: with one double point).

So the plane dial picks one Cayley–Klein measure, the one on a line. The nine plane geometries need two such choices (distance and angle), which the Cayley–Klein page already showed a single scalar law can't carry.

Known: Cayley 1859, Klein 1871, Beltrami 1868, Hilbert 1895; absolutes of the nine geometries (Yaglom 1979; Struve and Struve 2004). Ours: walls = absolute points, ruler = Cayley's distance, stated for our law. Verdict: a precise version of the hunch, with one correction.

4. Is the dial the eccentricity? No. It is the affine curvature.

Figure 6. Left: three ellipses with the same law (rescaling a). Middle: along d with k = 0, the conic's affine curvature is a straight line through the parabola; the eccentricity is not. Right: Kepler orbits with one angular momentum; energy picks the type.

  • Not the eccentricity. Rescaling a → λa gives the same law with (λk, λ²d), but a differently shaped ellipse (D2: e = 0.63 versus 0.88). Only the sign of e² − 1 is fixed by the dial (D3, 300 random dials). Eccentricity needs one more number, a ruler. Kepler shows it plainly: e² − 1 = 2EL²/μ² (D4), where the energy E is the plane dial (gravity page) and the angular momentum L is the extra number.
  • The affine curvature. In equi-affine geometry (lengths replaced by areas), conics are exactly the curves of constant curvature: positive for ellipses, zero for parabolas, negative for hyperbolas. For our conic it comes out as 2^(4/3) · κ, with κ = d − k²/4, sign and size, smoothly through the parabola (D1, eight dials, two points each). So the dial is a curvature after all, just not the ordinary one.

Known: constant affine curvature of conics and its sign (Blaschke 1923; Nomizu and Sasaki, Affine Differential Geometry, 1994); Kepler, Hamilton's hodograph, Milnor 1983. Ours: that this curvature is exactly our κ. Verdict: a lead worth following (section 6).

5. The other dials touch the conics once

Figure 7. Temperature turns a triangle into a circle only in the hot limit. The ℓᵖ dial passes through one conic, at p = 2. On the shape dial, every conic is the same round end.

  • k alone (d = 0): hyperbolas for every real k ≠ 0, the parabola at k = 0; ellipses only with imaginary k, the Cayley–Klein flip the why-i pages found.
  • Roundness by temperature (Maslov): the free-energy level set is a circle only in the hot limit; its out-of-roundness falls like T^(−1/2) (E1). Cold, it is the triangle, three straight lines.
  • Roundness by p (cross-polytope → sphere → cube): a conic only at p = 2 (E2). Its two ends are each made of two pairs of parallel lines: the flat setting's unit circle, twice.
  • Shape dial (Benzécri's space): ellipse, parabola and hyperbola are all one point, the round end where the Pick cubic form vanishes (Pick–Berwald). The other end is the triangle.

Known: all of it. Ours: the placement. Verdict: unifies; no new lead from these three.

6. Does this open a lead?

Yes, one, and it is worth following on its own merits. Section 4 puts the plane dial in affine differential geometry as the curvature of a curve. That same theory has exactly one more basic quantity for surfaces: the Pick cubic form, which is the shape dial (simplex page, section 7). The objects that carry both are the affine spheres (Calabi 1972; Cheng and Yau 1977, 1986; Loftin 2001): their constant mean curvature is elliptic, parabolic or hyperbolic, the quadrics are the ones with Pick form zero, and the hyperbolic ones sit over exactly the convex shapes of Benzécri's space. So the conjecture is: the plane dial and the shape dial are the two invariants of one known object, an affine sphere. Checked here only for curves, where there is no Pick form. The next step is to check surfaces: that the quadric affine spheres have mean curvature proportional to κ, and that moving the Pick form away from zero reproduces the shape dial's turn field.

The rest of this pass is bridges, not leads: the chord conic, the 3 × 3 placement, and the Cayley ruler are clean statements of known mathematics in our dial language.

Checks

Check What Result
A1–A6 chord conic: on the conic, chord rule = law (sympy exact), never degenerate, type = discriminant, walls at infinity, origin = addition pass
B1–B6 unit conic: size multiplies, directions compose by the law, completing the square = Cayley map, levels 0 and 1, flat case is parallel lines pass
C1–C4 ruler = Cayley distance in all three cases; Hilbert inside circle = Klein; parabola = same plane; one hyperbola branch ≠ pass
D1–D4 affine curvature = 2^(4/3)κ; eccentricity not invariant; sign(e² − 1) = sign(k² − 4d); Kepler e² − 1 = 2EL²/μ² pass
E1–E2 temperature gives a circle only hot; ℓᵖ is a conic only at p = 2 pass

Assumptions

  • Real conics and real dials, except where imaginary k is named.
  • "Circle" depends on a ruler: in the plain (x, y) ruler the chord conic is a circle only at (0, 1); after completing the square and rescaling, every no-wall setting is a circle.
  • The affine-curvature formula uses the equi-affine (area-preserving) normalization; under a → λa it scales like κ, so only its sign is a true invariant, as for κ.
